title: Cap. 7 Scholastici open: Sed missis — Lombard sufficienter/efficaciter
latin: Sed missis antiquioribus, ad Scholasticos & modernos Pontificios descendamus: Qui sic defendunt Christum pro omnibus mortuum, ut interim agnoscant pro Electis solis mortuum cum speciali intentione mortem suam eisdem applicandi ad infallibilem consecutionem vitae aeternae. 1. Ordiamur a Magistro Scholasticorum Petro Lombardo; Christus se in ara crucis obtulit pro omnibus, quantum ad pretii sufficientiam; sed pro electis tantum, quantum ad efficaciam, quia praedestinatis tantum salutem efficit, lib. 3. dist. 20 litt. c. Ratio quam subnectit Magister, cur Christus pro solis electis mortuus dicatur quantum ad efficaciam, est observatione dignissima. Non enim illam affert quam Pelagiani & Arminiani attulissent, scilicet quod illi tantum praevidebantur, pro libertate arbitrii sui per gratiam excitati, ut Christum sibi applicaturi, sed quod in illis tantum pro benignitate specialis suae misericordiae salutem effecerit. Quod autem morte sua in Electis effecit, proculdubio efficere decrevit. Atque haec est illa specialis intentio sub qua mortem Christi ad solos electos relatam, & ordinatam profitemur.
pass_a_gloss: But the ancients having been set aside, let us descend to the Scholastics and modern Pontificians: who so defend Christ as having died for all, that they meanwhile acknowledge him as having died for the Elect alone with a special intention of applying his death to the same unto the infallible attainment of eternal life. 1. Let us begin from the Master of the Scholastics, Peter Lombard; Christ offered himself on the altar of the cross for all, as to the sufficiency of the price; but for the elect only, as to efficacy, because he effects salvation only for the predestined, book 3, distinction 20, letter c. The reason which the Master subjoins, why Christ is said to have died for the elect alone as to efficacy, is most worthy of observation. For he does not bring that which the Pelagians and Arminians would have brought, namely that they alone were foreseen, excited by grace according to the freedom of their choice, as going to apply Christ to themselves, but that in them alone by the kindness of his special mercy he effected salvation. But what he effected by his death in the Elect, he doubtless decreed to effect. And this is that special intention under which we profess Christ's death related and ordained to the elect alone.
pass_b: Setting the older writers aside, we come down to the Scholastics and modern Romanists. They defend Christ as having died for all, yet they also grant he died for the elect alone with a special intention to apply that death to them so that eternal life follows without fail. 1. Start with Peter Lombard, master of the Scholastics: Christ offered himself on the cross's altar for all as to the price's sufficiency, but for the elect only as to efficacy, because he effects salvation only for the predestined (Sentences 3, dist. 20, litt. c). The reason he gives for calling Christ's death efficacious for the elect alone is worth marking. He does not say what Pelagians and Arminians would say — that only those were foreseen who, stirred by grace in free choice, would apply Christ to themselves — but that in them alone, by the kindness of special mercy, he wrought salvation. What his death wrought in the elect he surely decreed to work. That is the special intention under which we say Christ's death is related and ordained to the elect alone.

lemmas.gloss: the ancients having been set aside
as to the sufficiency of the price

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Aquinas — eternal ordination completed through Christ
latin: 2. Aquinas, part. 3. qu. 24. art. 4. Deus praeordinavit nostram salutem, ab aeterno praedestinando ut per Jesum Christum compleretur. Loquitur Aquinas de hominibus electis, atque asserit Deum ab aeterno ordinasse, ut eorum salus per Jesum Christum infallibiliter compleretur. Quaero igitur quomodo Christus huic aeternae ordinationi Patris sui sese conformem exhibuerit, si in passione sua salutifera ad electorum salutem infallibiliter efficiendam & complendam merita sua peculiari modo non applicaverit? Concedenda est itaque specialis intentio Dei hanc hostiam acceptantis, & Christi seipsum offerentis, restricta ad solos electos, quatenus passio Christi cum infallibili effectu salutis in singularibus personis conjungitur.
pass_a_gloss: 2. Aquinas, part 3, question 24, article 4. God preordained our salvation, by predestining from eternity that it should be completed through Jesus Christ. Aquinas speaks of elect human beings, and asserts that God from eternity ordained that their salvation should be completed through Jesus Christ infallibly. I ask therefore how Christ would have shown himself conformed to this eternal ordination of his Father, if in his saving passion he did not apply his merits in a peculiar manner unto infallibly effecting and completing the elect's salvation? There must therefore be conceded a special intention of God accepting this victim, and of Christ offering himself, restricted to the elect alone, insofar as Christ's passion is joined with an infallible effect of salvation in singular persons.
pass_b: 2. Aquinas (ST III q.24 a.4): God preordained our salvation by eternally predestining that it be completed through Jesus Christ. He is speaking of the elect, and he holds that from eternity God ordained their salvation to be finished through Christ without fail. How then could Christ have matched that eternal ordination of his Father if, in his saving passion, he did not apply his merits in a peculiar way to effect and complete the elect's salvation without fail? So we must grant a special intention — God accepting this victim, Christ offering himself — restricted to the elect alone, so far as Christ's passion is joined to an infallible saving effect in particular persons.

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Aquinas on merit — sufficiency vs efficacy; John 10:15
latin: 3. Idem, Quaest. Disp. De grat. Christi, art. 7. resp. ad 4. Meritum Christi quantum ad sufficientiam aequaliter se habet ad omnes, non autem quantum ad efficaciam: quod accidit partim ex libero arbitrio, partim ex Divina electione, per quam quibusdam misericorditer effectus meritorum Christi confertur, quibusdam vero justo judicio subtrahitur. Quod ait Aquinas, partim ex libero arbitrio accidere quod merita Christi, quantum ad efficaciam, non se habeant aequaliter ad omnes, id intelligendum est ex parte perditorum, qui libero arbitrio se avertunt a fonte salutis: Quod autem dixit, hanc inaequalitatem partim ex Divina electione accidere, id intelligendum est ex parte servatorum, qui, Deo secundum beneplacitum electionis specialiter illorum miserante, accipiunt a fonte salutis, quicquid necessarium est ad salutem illorum efficiendam. Hanc fuisse mentem Aquinatis patet ex responsione ad argumentum ultimum, ubi dicit, Hoc ipsum hominibus a Deo conferri gratis, quod effectum meriti Christi consequantur. Si effectus meritorum Christi ex Divina electione certis quibusdam personis misericorditer confertur, aliisque interim denegatur, quis dubitet Christum, Divinae electionis & suae vocationis optime conscium, pro iisdem personis seipsum & merita sua specialiter obtulisse, & pretio mortis in se sufficientissimo addidisse insuper efficacissimam & singularem voluntatis intentionem pro salute horum electorum operanda? Huc spectant illa, Johann. x. 15. Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis — nempe singulari quadam intentione eas efficaciter redimendi, liberandi, & ad vitam perducendi, uti ex toto discursu Servatoris eo in loco colligi potest.
pass_a_gloss: 3. The same, Disputed Questions On the Grace of Christ, article 7, reply to 4. Christ's merit as to sufficiency stands equally toward all, but not as to efficacy: which happens partly from free choice, partly from Divine election, through which to some the effect of Christ's merits is mercifully conferred, but from others it is withdrawn by just judgment. What Aquinas says — that it happens partly from free choice that Christ's merits as to efficacy do not stand equally toward all — is to be understood on the side of the lost, who by free choice turn themselves away from the fountain of salvation: but what he said — that this inequality happens partly from Divine election — is to be understood on the side of the saved, who, God specially having mercy on them according to the good pleasure of election, receive from the fountain of salvation whatever is necessary unto effecting their salvation. That this was Aquinas's mind is plain from the reply to the last argument, where he says, This very thing is conferred on human beings by God freely, that they obtain the effect of Christ's merit. If the effect of Christ's merits is mercifully conferred from Divine election on certain persons, and meanwhile denied to others, who would doubt that Christ, most well aware of Divine election and of his own calling, specially offered himself and his merits for those same persons, and to the price of death most sufficient in itself added besides a most efficacious and singular intention of will for working the salvation of these elect? Those words look hither, John 10:15. I lay down my life for my sheep — namely with a certain singular intention of efficaciously redeeming, freeing, and leading them unto life, as can be gathered from the Savior's whole discourse in that place.
pass_b: 3. The same Aquinas, On the Grace of Christ (disp. q.), art. 7 ad 4: Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy. That inequality comes partly from free choice, partly from divine election, by which the effect of Christ's merits is mercifully given to some and justly withheld from others. When he says free choice partly explains unequal efficacy, read that of the lost, who turn themselves from the fountain of salvation. When he says divine election partly explains it, read that of the saved, who, under God's special mercy according to election's good pleasure, receive from that fountain whatever is needed to effect their salvation. His reply to the last objection shows the mind: God freely confers on people that they obtain the effect of Christ's merit. If election mercifully gives that effect to some and denies it to others, who can doubt that Christ — knowing election and his own calling — specially offered himself and his merits for those persons, and added to a price already sufficient in itself a most effectual, singular will to work their salvation? John 10:15 points the same way: I lay down my life for my sheep — with a singular intention to redeem, free, and bring them to life, as the whole discourse there shows.

lemmas.form: Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis
lemmas.gloss: I lay down my life for my sheep

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Scotus and Hugh of St Victor on elect-directed passion
latin: 4. Scotus in 3. Sentent. dist. 19. quest. unica, multa habet quae valde conducunt ad sententiam nostram illustrandam, illud inprimis, Sicut Verbum praevidit passionem suam Patri offerendam pro electis, sic eam efficaciter obtulit in effectum, & tota Trinitas pro eis passionem efficaciter acceptavit, & pro nullis aliis fuit efficaciter oblata, nec ab aeterno acceptata. Agnoscit Scotus, ex aeterno decreto totius Trinitatis passionem Christi fuisse singulari quodam modo & speciali intentione oblatam & acceptatam pro electis. 5. Hugo de S. Victore, De Sacr. fid. lib. 1. part. 8. cap. 7. Ubi tractationem instituit De passione Christi, sic scribit, Natura humana per peccatum corrupta fuit, & tota per peccatum damnationi debita erat, & idcirco, si tota damnata fuisset, injustitia non fuisset. Venit autem gratia, & elegit quosdam de massa universitatis per misericordiam ad salutem, quosdam autem per justitiam deseruit ad damnationem. Aperte docet Hugo, Christum in mundum venientem, & pro peccatis humani generis sese offerentem, habuisse respectum singularem ad electos, quos de massa universitatis elegit, quosque ad salutem pro aeterno Dei beneplacito per merita mortis suae perducere decrevit, & de facto semper perducit.
pass_a_gloss: 4. Scotus on the Sentences, book 3, distinction 19, the single question, has many things which greatly help to illustrate our opinion, this first of all: Just as the Word foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the elect, so he efficaciously offered it unto effect, and the whole Trinity efficaciously accepted the passion for them, and for no others was it efficaciously offered, nor accepted from eternity. Scotus acknowledges that from the eternal decree of the whole Trinity Christ's passion was offered and accepted for the elect in a certain singular manner and with a special intention. 5. Hugh of Saint Victor, On the Sacraments of the Faith, book 1, part 8, chapter 7. Where he institutes a treatment On the passion of Christ, he writes thus: Human nature was corrupted through sin, and the whole was due to damnation through sin, and therefore, if the whole had been damned, it would not have been injustice. But grace came, and chose some from the mass of the universe through mercy unto salvation, but deserted some through justice unto damnation. Hugh openly teaches that Christ coming into the world, and offering himself for the sins of the human race, had a singular respect toward the elect, whom he chose from the mass of the universe, and whom he decreed to lead unto salvation by the merits of his death according to God's eternal good pleasure, and in fact always leads.
pass_b: 4. Scotus (Sentences III, dist. 19, single q.) has much that illustrates our view. First: just as the Word foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the elect, so he offered it effectually unto its effect, and the whole Trinity effectually accepted that passion for them; for no others was it effectually offered or eternally accepted. So Scotus grants that by the Trinity's eternal decree Christ's passion was offered and accepted for the elect in a singular way, with special intention. 5. Hugh of St Victor (On the Sacraments I.8.7), treating Christ's passion: Human nature was corrupted by sin and wholly owed to damnation; if all had been damned, that would not have been injustice. But grace came and chose some from the mass of the whole by mercy unto salvation, and left some by justice unto damnation. Hugh teaches plainly that Christ, coming and offering himself for the race's sins, kept a singular eye on the elect he chose from that mass, whom he decreed — and in fact always does — to bring to salvation by his death's merits according to God's eternal good pleasure.

lemmas.gloss: from the mass of the universe

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Cajetan on Romans 8 — special donation to the elect
latin: 6. Cajetanus, in Rom. viii. explicans haec verba, Qui proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus eum tradidit, quomodo non cum illo omnia nobis donabit? sic scribit, Animadverterat Paulus, quod praeallegata ratio tot donorum non efficaciter inferebat Deum omnia in bonum electis cooperari, sed Deum illis cooperari in bonum, & propterea ut efficaciter concluderet quod OMNIA, adjinxit, quod Deus liberaliter donavit etiam Filium pro electis, ut hinc inferret quod omnia cum Filio electis donata sunt. Non possunt haec dicta Cajetani ad illam universalem Christi donationem accommodari, qua toti mundo datus ex aequo intelligitur: nam hoc posito, Deus omnia omnibus hominibus ex aequo daret: quod manifeste falsum est. Specialis ergo quaedam donatio necessario concedenda est, juxta quam Christus solis electis datus intelligatur, & quae sola trahat post se infallibilem & certissimam donationem omnium rerum ad salutem necessariarum.
pass_a_gloss: 6. Cajetan, on Romans 8, explaining these words, He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also give us all things? writes thus: Paul had noticed that the previously alleged reason of so many gifts did not efficaciously infer that God works all things unto good for the elect, but that God works with them unto good, and therefore, that he might efficaciously conclude that ALL THINGS, he added that God liberally gave even the Son for the elect, that from this he might infer that all things with the Son have been given to the elect. These sayings of Cajetan cannot be accommodated to that universal donation of Christ by which he is understood given to the whole world equally: for this being posited, God would give all things to all human beings equally: which is manifestly false. A certain special donation must therefore necessarily be conceded, according to which Christ is understood given to the elect alone, and which alone draws after itself an infallible and most certain donation of all things necessary unto salvation.
pass_b: 6. Cajetan on Romans 8: He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things? Paul saw that the earlier chain of gifts did not yet prove effectually that God works all things for the elect's good — only that he works with them unto good. So, to conclude ALL THINGS effectually, he added that God freely gave even the Son for the elect, and from that inferred that with the Son all things are given to them. Cajetan's words cannot be bent to a universal gift of Christ given equally to the whole world: if that were so, God would give all things equally to every human being — which is plainly false. A special donation must be granted, under which Christ is given to the elect alone, and which alone carries after it an infallible, most certain gift of everything needed for salvation.

lemmas.gloss: delivered him up for us all

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici: Stapleton and Estius — efficacy for future friends / elect
latin: 7. Stapletonus, Promptuar. Moral. Dominic. 2. post Pasch. pag. 254. Christus moriens efficaciter quidem pro solis amicis mortuus est, idque pro futuris amicis post conversionem singulorum, non pro iis qui antea amici fuerant. Non veretur hic Papista singularem Christi morientis intentionem quoad Electos agnoscere. Nam hi sunt illi amici post conversionem futuri, pro quibus efficaciter redimendis Christus animam suam posuit, quando cum caeteris impii, inimici, peccatores, in peccatis mortui exstiterunt. Mortuus quidem dicitur pro omnibus hominibus, sed quoad sufficientiam: pro ovibus autem, sive electis suis, quoad hanc efficaciam, id est, cum singulari intentione ex merito mortis suae dandi illis gratiam illam efficacem unde credant & salventur. 8. Estius, ad illa verba, Tit. ii. 14. Qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, Hoc est, inquit, qui in assumpta carne tradidit semetipsum, sive pro omnibus hominibus, sive speciatim pro electis, in quorum persona Paulus saepe loquitur. Nam pretium mortis Christi sufficit quidem omnibus redimendis & salvandis, sed solis ad salutem applicatur electis. Hactenus ille. Duo hic innuit Estius: Unum, Christi oblationem generalem respectum ad omnes, ac specialem ad electos habuisse; Alterum, Hunc specialem respectum in eo constitui oportere, quod cum intentione certi applicandi sit conjunctus. Non enim dixit, Soli Electi hanc mortem Christi viribus liberi arbitrii sibi applicant ad salutem, sed, Hisce solis applicatur ad salutem, Dei scilicet eligentis, & hoc tantum bonum electis suis ex Christi morte intendentis, favore speciali.
pass_a_gloss: 7. Stapleton, Moral Promptuary, Second Sunday after Easter, page 254. Christ dying indeed died efficaciously for friends alone, and that for future friends after the conversion of individuals, not for those who had been friends beforehand. This Papist does not fear to acknowledge the singular intention of Christ dying as to the Elect. For these are those future friends after conversion, for whose efficacious redeeming Christ laid down his life, when with the rest they stood as impious, enemies, sinners, dead in sins. He is indeed said to have died for all human beings, but as to sufficiency: but for his sheep, or his elect, as to this efficacy, that is, with a singular intention from the merit of his death of giving them that efficacious grace whence they believe and are saved. 8. Estius, on those words, Titus 2:14. Who gave himself for us — This is, he says, who in assumed flesh delivered himself up, whether for all human beings, or specially for the elect, in whose person Paul often speaks. For the price of Christ's death indeed suffices for all to be redeemed and saved, but is applied unto salvation to the elect alone. Thus far he. Estius here hints two things: One, that Christ's oblation had a general respect toward all, and a special toward the elect; Another, that this special respect ought to be constituted in this, that it is joined with an intention of applying it certainly. For he did not say, The Elect alone apply this death of Christ to themselves unto salvation by the powers of free choice, but, It is applied unto salvation to these alone, namely by the favor of God electing, and intending this good alone for his elect from Christ's death, by special favor.
pass_b: 7. Stapleton (Moral Promptuary, Second Sunday after Easter, p. 254): Dying, Christ died effectually for friends alone — for friends-to-be after each one's conversion, not for those who were already friends. This Romanist does not shrink from granting Christ's dying a singular intention toward the elect. They are the future friends after conversion for whose effectual redemption he laid down his life while, with the rest, they were still ungodly, enemies, sinners, dead in sins. He is said to have died for all humans as to sufficiency; for his sheep — his elect — as to this efficacy, that is, with a singular intention, from his death's merit, to give them the effectual grace by which they believe and are saved. 8. Estius on Titus 2:14, Who gave himself for us: that is, who in assumed flesh delivered himself up, whether for all humans or specially for the elect, in whose person Paul often speaks. Christ's death-price suffices to redeem and save all, yet is applied unto salvation to the elect alone. Estius thus hints two things: Christ's offering had a general respect to all and a special to the elect; and that special respect must be defined as joined to an intention of applying it with certainty. He did not say the elect alone apply Christ's death to themselves by free choice's powers, but that it is applied unto salvation to them alone — by electing God, intending this good for his elect from Christ's death by special favor.

lemmas.gloss: is applied unto salvation to the elect alone

title: Cap. 7 Scholastici close: Suarez and Vasquez before Reformed Theologi nostri
latin: 9. Venio ad Jesuitas, qui utcunque universalem gratiam, & universalem redemtionem defendant, tamen hanc specialem & efficacem salutiferae passionis ordinationem & intentionem quoad solos electos non audent inficiari. Pro reliquis loquantur duo ex antesignanis, Suarez, & Vasquez. Suarez, in 3. Aquin. qu. 19. Disp. pag. 635. §. 41. Sicut Christus diversimode pro hominibus oravit, ita diversimode meruit, aliis sufficienter, aliis efficaciter. Propter quod, licet omnium sit universalis Redemtor, & sufficiens causa salutis, speciali tamen modo est causa efficax salutis eorum, quos sibi facit obedientes. Incredibile enim est, non aliter obtulisse Christum sua merita pro illis, quos sciebat esse electos a Patre, quam pro aliis, cum videret esse Patris voluntatem ut illi infallibiliter salvarentur, & non alii. Largitur nobis Suarez, Christi mortem ac merita esse efficacia ad salutem electorum ex speciali modo oblationis & voluntate offerentis, non ex casuali seu contingente actu humanae voluntatis eam apprehendentis. 10. Vasquez hanc specialem Christi intentionem quoad electos in applicatione meritorum suorum clare agnoscit, in 1. Aquinat. qu. 23. disp. 49. cap. 3. pag. 687. Ego non dubito Christum peculiari oratione & voluntate merita sua illis applicasse, qui praedestinati & electi fuerunt. Idem, in 3. Aquinat. qu. 19. disp. 77. cap. 5. pag. 384. inducit Andream Vegam asserentem, merita Christi non omnibus efficaciter prodesse, quia pro illis (quibus non prosunt) efficaciter Christus non oravit, nec obtulit suam passionem. Habemus igitur non solum antiquos Patres, sed ipsos etiam Papistas neotericos fatentes, quod nos demonstrare conamur, nimirum, Christi mortem sic a Deo constitutam universalem causam salutis omnibus applicabilem, ut interim, per specialem quandam intentionem offerentis & acceptantis, constituatur particularis causa salutis omnibus & solis electis infallibiliter & singulariter applicanda. Vide etiam Malderi Antisynod. pag. 138.
pass_a_gloss: 9. I come to the Jesuits, who however they defend universal grace and universal redemption, yet do not dare to deny this special and efficacious ordination and intention of the saving passion as to the elect alone. For the rest let two of the foremost speak, Suarez and Vasquez. Suarez, on Aquinas part 3, question 19, Disputation, page 635, section 41. Just as Christ prayed in diverse manners for human beings, so he merited in diverse manners, for some sufficiently, for others efficaciously. Wherefore, although he is the universal Redeemer of all, and a sufficient cause of salvation, yet in a special manner he is the efficacious cause of the salvation of those whom he makes obedient to himself. For it is incredible that Christ offered his merits no otherwise for those whom he knew to be elect by the Father than for others, when he saw it to be the Father's will that they be saved infallibly, and not others. Suarez grants us that Christ's death and merits are efficacious unto the elect's salvation from the special manner of offering and the will of the offerer, not from a casual or contingent act of the human will apprehending it. 10. Vasquez clearly acknowledges this special intention of Christ as to the elect in the application of his merits, on Aquinas 1, question 23, disputation 49, chapter 3, page 687. I do not doubt that Christ by a peculiar prayer and will applied his merits to those who were predestined and elect. The same, on Aquinas 3, question 19, disputation 77, chapter 5, page 384, brings in Andreas Vega asserting that Christ's merits do not profit all efficaciously, because for those (to whom they do not profit) Christ did not pray efficaciously, nor offer his passion. We have therefore not only the ancient Fathers, but even the newer Papists themselves confessing what we are trying to demonstrate, namely that Christ's death is so constituted by God a universal cause of salvation applicable to all, that meanwhile, through a certain special intention of the offerer and accepter, it is constituted a particular cause of salvation to be applied infallibly and singularly to all and only the elect. See also Malderus, Antisynod, page 138.
pass_b: 9. Next the Jesuits. However they defend universal grace and universal redemption, they dare not deny this special, effectual ordination and intention of the saving passion toward the elect alone. Let two chiefs speak: Suarez and Vasquez. Suarez on Aquinas III q.19 (Disp. p. 635 §41): as Christ prayed diversely for humans, so he merited diversely — for some sufficiently, for others effectually. So though he is everyone's universal Redeemer and a sufficient cause of salvation, in a special way he is the effectual cause of salvation for those he makes obedient. It is incredible he offered his merits no differently for those he knew the Father had elect than for others, when he saw the Father's will was that they be saved without fail, and not others. Suarez thus grants that Christ's death and merits save the elect from the special mode of offering and the offerer's will — not from a chance act of human will laying hold of them. 10. Vasquez clearly owns this special intention toward the elect in applying his merits (on Aquinas I q.23, disp. 49, c.3, p. 687): I do not doubt Christ by peculiar prayer and will applied his merits to those predestined and elect. The same on Aquinas III q.19, disp. 77, c.5, p. 384, cites Andreas Vega: Christ's merits do not profit all effectually, because for those they do not profit he did not pray effectually or offer his passion. So not only the old Fathers but even newer Romanists confess what we aim to prove: God constituted Christ's death a universal saving cause applicable to all, yet by a special intention of offerer and accepter it is also a particular saving cause to be applied without fail, and singularly, to all and only the elect. See also Malderus, Antisynod, p. 138.

lemmas.gloss: for some sufficiently, for others efficaciously
